chunks: "I use a heat sink when the board alone can't keep the junction below its limit at the worst-case ambient and power.
The test is a calculation: junction temperature is ambient plus power times the total thermal resistance.
Suppose a TO-220 FET dissipates 3 watts in a 50 degrees Celsius enclosure and I want to keep the junction at 110 degrees Celsius, which gives margin under a 150 degrees Celsius limit.
That allows 60 degrees of rise, so the total resistance has to be 20 kelvin per watt or less. A TO-220 in free air is more like 60. With junction-to-case at 1.
5 and an insulating pad at 0. 5, the heat sink needs to be 18 K/W or better, which a modest extruded sink can do, and a fan would help further.
Before I add one I look at the cheaper options: dissipate less, for example with a buck instead of an LDO; add copper, thermal vias and airflow; or bolt the part to the enclosure.

A heat sink makes sense when the dissipation is a few watts or more in a package that can't spread it on the board, when the enclosure is hot, or when the part has a tab designed to be mounted to one.
Then the details: thermal paste or pad, an insulator if the tab is at a voltage, mounting pressure, and keeping a floating metal sink away from switching nodes, because it acts like an antenna."
